claims.text: Protective oxide development and retention in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by preferential oxidation of elements with lower redox potential, such as chromium.
Preferential chromium oxidation rapidly forms a stable, adherent subscale.
The chromium-rich subscale kinetically limits oxygen diffusion and subsequent oxidation.
The initial material can be an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn bulk alloy.
The oxide-forming elements are uniformly distributed in the initial alloy.
Relevant oxidation conditions include oxygen-rich atmospheres above 500 °C, including 900–1100 °C, over extended durations.
Atmospheric oxidation of CoCrFeNiMn alloys produces a layered film with a chromium-rich inner oxide and a manganese-rich outer oxide.
The chromium-rich inner oxide acts as a barrier to further oxygen ingress.
Differences in redox potential and oxidation kinetics among alloying elements govern selective oxidation.
The element with the lowest redox potential, exemplified by chromium, migrates to the surface and oxidizes first.
Selective oxidation creates a dense protective oxide sublayer.
Retardation of oxygen diffusion through that sublayer controls the overall oxidation process.
A chromium-containing HEA will develop a protective chromium-rich oxide layer under the stated conditions.
The chromium-containing HEA will exhibit lower mass gain and a more stable oxide structure than alloys with inadequate chromium.
Lower-chromium HEAs or traditional alloys lacking multicomponent interactions will oxidize faster and form less-adherent scales.
The proposed mechanism applies principally to high-temperature, oxygen-rich environments.
The mechanism may be less effective at lower temperatures or in sulfur- or carbon-rich atmospheres.
Polycrystallinity, surface heterogeneity, and high-temperature phase instability can alter oxide structures and protective behavior.
Minor-element variations and phase instabilities may complicate preferential oxidation in HEAs.
Comparable protective behavior in reduced-chromium and standard samples, or absence of a chromium-rich sublayer correlated with resistance, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
